name: Bone-extending procedures
lead: Bone-extending procedures, usually called limb lengthening or height surgery, add stature by lengthening the leg bones. A surgeon cuts the tibia or femur and the pieces are separated gradually so new bone forms in the gap, a method called distraction osteogenesis [1]. People choose it to gain permanent height and, in some cases, to correct leg shape or body proportion [2].

The technique grew out of work by Gavriil Ilizarov from the 1950s, who developed external fixators and workable separation rates [1][2]. The first reported cosmetic case, in Volgograd in 1992, lengthened a healthy patient's tibia by 6 cm over 11 months [2]. Current options include external frames, spring-tensioned devices and fully implantable motorized nails such as the Fitbone [1].

Height surgery has drawn media attention. A 2026 New York Times article, discussed on Hacker News, was titled "Height Surgery for Men Can Add Inches but Has Risks" [3]. Published complication rates come from limb lengthening in general rather than from cosmetic cases specifically [1].

angle.text: Surgeons lengthen the tibia or femur by gradual distraction, producing a lasting gain in standing height; the first cosmetic case added 6 cm [2]. It is the route people take when they want added height that does not depend on footwear or posture, and it can also change leg-to-torso proportion [2].

infobox: 17 and older, after growth plates close[2]

paras: Distraction osteogenesis has five phases: osteotomy, in which the bone is cut and the device fitted; a latency period of about seven days; distraction at roughly 1 mm per day, usually in two steps; consolidation while the new bone hardens; and removal of the device in a second operation [1].

Devices include manually turned external rods, spring-tensioned frames that separate bones continuously, and the Fitbone, a fully implantable motorized nail. Wikipedia's summary lists accurate correction, less scar tissue and lower infection risk among the Fitbone's reported advantages, and says patients report it as more comfortable than mechanical systems [1].

Anthropometric cosmetology lists indications including legs short relative to body length, X- or O-shaped leg curvature, and psychological distress about height [2]. Operations are professionally recommended from age 17, after the growth zones have closed [2].
In India, where height is described as highly attractive and linked to marriage and career prospects, cosmetic lengthening has been in demand [1].

Bernhard von Langenbeck proposed bone lengthening in 1869, and Alessandro Codivilla published the first clinical attempt in 1905, treating 26 people with high complication rates [1]. Ilizarov studied the method in more than 15,000 people from the 1950s, developed external fixators and defined optimal distraction rates [1]. In 1965 he determined that bone fragments could be pulled apart without losing alignment [2].

Kaplunov and Yegorov used the method for strictly cosmetic purposes in Volgograd in 1992, lengthening a healthy patient's tibia by 6 cm over 11 months; Yegorov, Chernov and Nekrasov later wrote the first scientific book on the field, Orthopedic Cosmetology [2].
For distraction osteogenesis in general, Wikipedia cites overall infection of 5%, bone growing in the wrong direction in 7-9%, hardware failure in 3-4.5% and protocol failure in 4.5% [1].

In India, some patients reported that surgeons misled them about complications, and some who developed infections needed further surgery months later to walk again; some gained less height than expected [1]. China's Ministry of Health banned limb lengthening in 2006 after operations with serious side effects [1].

Height surgery is discussed in height-focused communities as the durable alternative to lifts or posture work, with attention to cost, recovery time and surgeon choice. It also appears in popular media, including a video discussed on Lemmy as a dangerous plastic surgery trend [4] and the Hacker News thread on the 2026 New York Times article [3].
No studies found on cosmetic height surgery specifically. Complication figures above come from limb lengthening for deformity and trauma [1].

card.summary: Surgery that gradually lengthens leg bones to add permanent height.
card.aka: Limb lengthening, height surgery, leg lengthening
card.note: Major surgery with months of recovery and a recognised complication rate.

quick.overview:
Bone-extending procedures cut a leg bone and slowly pull the ends apart so new bone grows in between. The result is permanent added height, historically several centimetres per bone.

The first cosmetic case in 1992 added 6 cm to a tibia over 11 months.
quick.mechanism: Distraction osteogenesis: osteotomy, a short wait, lengthening of about 1 mm per day with an external frame or motorized nail, then months of bone consolidation.
quick.risks: Reported complications include infection (about 5%), poor bone healing, hardware failure and nerve injury. Regulation varies; China banned the procedure in 2006.
